reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A recurrent deletion of approximately 1.6 Mb generated by non-allelic homologous recombination between flanking low-copy repeats
Mild to moderate intellectual disability and developmental delay, particularly affecting speech
Substantially increased risk of psychiatric illness, notably schizophrenia, as well as autism spectrum disorder and anxiety
Microcephaly and a long, narrow face with other subtle dysmorphic features are often described
The reciprocal duplication of the same interval also exists and carries its own neurodevelopmental risks
Expressivity is variable and penetrance incomplete, so an inherited deletion may be found in a mildly affected relative
Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive can occur in infancy
Chromosomal microarray is the first-line diagnostic test
reference.pathophysiology: The 3q29 region is flanked by segmental duplications that misalign at meiosis and predispose to non-allelic homologous recombination, generating a recurrent deletion or its reciprocal duplication. The deleted interval contains several dosage-sensitive genes with roles in synaptic function and neuronal signalling, and their haploinsufficiency is thought to underlie the neurodevelopmental and psychiatric phenotype. The relatively high risk of schizophrenia is one of the strongest single-locus associations known. Variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance reflect additional genetic and environmental modifiers acting on the affected pathways.
additionalDifferentials: Other recurrent copy-number syndromes associated with schizophrenia risk (e.g. 22q11.2 deletion, 15q13.3 deletion)
Primary psychiatric disorder without an identifiable copy-number change
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray as first-line to detect and size the deletion
FISH or MLPA to confirm the finding
Parental studies to determine inheritance and counsel recurrence risk
Psychiatric evaluation and monitoring given the elevated risk of psychosis
Echocardiography where a cardiac anomaly is suspected clinically
redFlags: Emerging psychotic symptoms in adolescence or adulthood
Faltering growth or significant feeding difficulty in infancy
reference.prognosis: Most individuals have mild to moderate learning difficulty and can achieve a degree of independence with support, but the markedly raised risk of schizophrenia and other psychiatric illness is an important influence on the lifelong outlook. Early developmental intervention and psychiatric vigilance in adolescence are therefore central to care.
pitfalls: Overlooking the substantial psychiatric risk and failing to monitor for emerging psychosis in adolescence and adulthood
Assuming an inherited deletion is benign because a relative appears mildly affected
Attributing all difficulties to the deletion and missing coexisting treatable conditions
Neglecting speech-language support that can materially improve function
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Individualised early developmental support, with speech and language therapy for the prominent expressive-speech delay plus occupational and educational input for intellectual disability
Longitudinal psychiatric surveillance for emerging schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder and anxiety, with early antipsychotic or psychological treatment when symptoms arise
Echocardiography and cardiology review where a congenital cardiac anomaly is suspected clinically
Coordinated multidisciplinary follow-up across clinical genetics, developmental paediatrics, psychiatry and allied therapies
Genetic counselling with parental chromosomal microarray or FISH to determine inheritance and counsel recurrence risk, given variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance
Prompt escalation to psychiatric services at the first signs of a psychotic prodrome, reflecting the strong single-locus schizophrenia association
